abstract: <jats:p>Golden samphire [Limbarda crithmodes (L.) Dumort], a perennial, edible Mediterranean halophytic specie, is recognised for its richness in biologically active compounds and its associated health benefits. Despite its potential, it remains largely underexplored in Croatia. This study investigates the effect of plant’s phenological stage—vegetative phase (June), pre-flowering (July), and full flowering (August)—on its phenolic profile (total phenolics, flavonoids, and tannins using spectrophotometry, and individual phenolic compounds using ultra-high performance liquid chromatography and antioxidant potential (using three complementary in vitro assays)). Total phenolics, flavonoids and related antioxidant activity progressively increased from June to August. Among the 18 identified phenolic compounds, chlorogenic acid was the most abundant (355 to 455 µg/g), reaching its highest concentration in the August sample, while among flavonoids it was quercetin (32 to 34 µg/g). These findings suggest that golden samphire collected in the late summer flowering stage exhibits the highest phenolic and antioxidant potential, and that chlorogenic acid, likely acting in synergy with other phenolics, may play the key role in the plant’s biological activity, reinforcing its potential for future applications.</jats:p>
title: Phenolic Antioxidants in the Adriatic Halophyte Limbarda crithmoides: Variation Across Phenological Stages

abstract: <jats:p>Fungi are recognized as indigenous microbes in natural hypersaline habitats. Aspergillus sp, among other fungi, is predominant in those environments; however, their adaptative abilities are recently studied. This study analyzes the transcriptomic response of an obligate halophile Aspergillus loretoensis under two salinity conditions (4% and 15% NaCl). This fungus shows stress under the low NaCl concentration tested since it overexpresses genes like SOD2 (oxidative stress and oxygen toxicity), ASG (resistance to salinity), and transmembrane transport (ZRT2, OAC1, PMA1, ZRC1, SNQ2, MCH4, YO075, SIT1). Meanwhile, at 15% NaCl, the up-regulated genes at 15% NaCl were related to osmolytes transport (STL1, HXT13, ZRT1), carbohydrate transport, and metabolism (MAL11, PK1, ITR1), all suggesting their adaptive conditions. This fungus expresses interesting metabolic enzymes with potential uses in biotechnology as invertases, isomerases, maltases, and lipases. As well it showed biosynthetic pathways related to oil degradation and antibiotic production.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The moderate halophile <jats:italic>Halomonas elongata</jats:italic> can assimilate a variety of sugars and/or amino acids derived from bio-wastes as carbon and/or nitrogen sources. Thus, <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> could be a practical cell factory for bioproduction of fine chemicals such as ectoine. In protein-rich bio-wastes, putrefactive non-volatile amines could be formed as biogenic amines by decarboxylation of amino acids during biological rotten processes and be a considerable toxicological risk. Therefore, we investigated whether <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> can assimilate major putrefactive non-volatile amines, Histamine and Tyramine, as carbon and/or nitrogen sources or not. Comparative analysis using closely related <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> strains, OUT30018 and DSM2581<jats:sup>T</jats:sup>, revealed that <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> OUT30018 can assimilate both Histamine and Tyramine, and produce ectoine under high salinity, while <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> DSM2581<jats:sup>T</jats:sup> cannot. Thus, <jats:italic>H. elongata</jats:italic> OUT30018 would be a one of the most promising cell factories to produce fine chemicals such as ectoine from the putrefactive non-volatile amines in protein-rich bio-waste.</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>
                      Protein splicing is a post‐translational process facilitated by an intervening polypeptide called an intein, or internal protein. The intein is located between two flanking polypeptides, called exteins. The intein catalyzes its excision from the extein concomitant with the ligation of the exteins. The extremophile
                      <jats:italic>Haloferax volcanii</jats:italic>
                      grows in high salt environments. We are interested in the salt‐dependence of the protein splicing and nuclease activity of the intein that has invaded its DNA Polymerase beta gene. We have shown that we can induce protein splicing of the intein
                      <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                      as a function of salt concentration and time. The intein has an intervening homing endonuclease domain and we are interested to learn if mutations within this domain would influence splicing. Characterization of a conditionally‐active nuclease may have utility in biotechnology applications.
